question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L\{u(t-2)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-2)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=2,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-2)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-2s}\,L\{g(t+2)\},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+2) & =sin\,(\pi (t+2)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t+2\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+2)\} & =L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-2)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-2s}\,L\{g(t+2)\} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{s}^{2}+{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
